A Kitchen Designed Around How You Live

The best kitchens do more than look beautiful—they make everyday life easier. When your kitchen feels cramped, lacks storage, has an awkward layout, or simply no longer fits the way you live, a thoughtful remodel can completely change how you use your home.

At Renovations and Dependable Building, we help homeowners throughout Blacksburg, Christiansburg, and the New River Valley create kitchens that are both beautiful and practical. Every project starts with understanding what is working, what isn't, and what would make the space function better for you. From cabinetry and storage to layout, lighting, finishes, and the details that make a kitchen feel like your own, we guide you through the process from planning through construction.

Quality Craftsmanship, Thoughtfully Coordinated

A successful kitchen remodel depends on more than beautiful finishes. It takes careful planning, skilled craftsmanship, and coordination between everyone involved in the project.

At Renovations and Dependable Building, we manage the many moving parts of your kitchen remodel—from cabinetry, countertops, tile, flooring, and finish carpentry to plumbing, electrical work, lighting, and appliance installation. We work with trusted trade partners and suppliers throughout the New River Valley and coordinate the details so each phase of the project is ready for the next.

Just as importantly, we pay attention to how all of those pieces come together. Cabinet placement, storage, lighting, appliance locations, trim, and finishing details are considered as part of the whole kitchen—not as separate tasks. The result is a space that feels cohesive, functions well, and is built for everyday life.

A finished basement can add valuable living space without changing the footprint of your home. Whether you need a comfortable family room, space for guests, a home office, a hobby area, or a flexible combination of uses, the right plan can turn an underused lower level into a space that feels like a natural extension of the rest of your home.

We also think about how the basement connects to the rest of the home—how you enter the space, how rooms flow together, where storage belongs, and how the finished area will actually be used. The goal is to create a lower level that feels intentional and comfortable, not simply like an unfinished basement that has been covered up.

Make More of the Space You Already Have

An unfinished or underused attic can hold more potential than you might think. With the right planning, attic space can become a home office, bedroom, hobby room, bonus room, or flexible living area that adds function without expanding the footprint of your home.

At Renovations & Dependable Building, we help homeowners throughout Blacksburg and the New River Valley evaluate attic spaces and determine what may be possible. Every project starts with understanding how you want to use the space and then looking carefully at practical considerations such as access, ceiling height, insulation, lighting, storage, and heating and cooling.

From framing, flooring, drywall, electrical work, built-in storage, and finish carpentry to stairs and other access improvements, we coordinate the details needed to turn an unfinished attic into a comfortable, usable part of your home.

Thoughtful Planning for Unique Spaces

Attic remodeling comes with a different set of considerations than working in a standard room. Sloped ceilings, limited headroom, stair access, insulation, natural light, heating and cooling, and storage all affect how comfortable and functional the finished space can be.

At Renovations and Dependable Building, we look carefully at the existing conditions before planning the remodel. Depending on the space, the work may include framing, flooring, drywall, electrical updates, lighting, insulation, built-in storage, finish carpentry, and improvements to stairs or access.

The goal is to make the most of the space that is actually there. Thoughtful planning can turn awkward corners, low rooflines, and underused areas into useful features rather than limitations—creating an attic that feels intentional, comfortable, and connected to the rest of the home.

Beyond Grab Bars: Smart Aging-in-Place Ideas to Consider During a Remodel

When people hear the phrase “aging in place,” one of the first things that may come to mind is a grab bar in the shower. And while bathroom safety is certainly part of the conversation, aging-in-place remodeling can be much more than that. At its best, it’s about creating a home that is comfortable, easy to navigate, and functional for the people who live there — not just today, but for years to come.

If you’re already planning a major remodel, it may be the perfect time to think about a few design decisions that could make your home easier to live in later. Many of them don’t look like “aging-in-place features” at all. They simply look like thoughtful design.

1. Look for Opportunities to Reduce Barriers

Small changes in elevation can become bigger obstacles over time.

When remodeling, consider where you may be able to reduce steps, high thresholds, or abrupt transitions between rooms. This might mean creating a lower-threshold or curbless shower, improving the transition between indoor and outdoor living spaces, or thinking ahead about an entry into the home that could eventually be accessed without stairs.

You may never need a completely step-free home. But reducing unnecessary barriers can make a home more convenient for everyone — including young children, visiting family members, someone recovering from an injury, or a homeowner carrying groceries through the door.

2. Give Yourself Room to Move

A beautiful room can still be frustrating if navigating it requires squeezing between furniture, fixtures, cabinets and doorways. During a remodel, think beyond whether everything technically “fits.” Consider how comfortably someone can move through the space.

In a kitchen, that might mean providing generous pathways around an island rather than making the island as large as possible. In a bathroom, it could mean creating more open space around the vanity, toilet or shower. Wider doorways and less congested hallways can also make a home easier to navigate.

Good circulation feels comfortable now and provides more flexibility if mobility needs change later.

3. Make the Shower Work Harder

The bathroom is one of the most obvious places to incorporate aging-in-place ideas — but the result doesn't have to look institutional. A spacious walk-in or curbless shower can be a beautiful design feature while also eliminating a high step over a tub or shower curb. A built-in bench or ledge provides convenience today and could offer seating later. A handheld showerhead adds flexibility for people of different heights and abilities.

Even the placement of shower controls matters. Being able to turn on the water without stepping directly underneath it is a small detail that can make the shower more comfortable to use.

And here's something homeowners may not see at all: blocking inside the walls.

If the bathroom walls are already open during construction, additional reinforcement can sometimes be installed in strategic locations. That creates secure mounting locations if a homeowner decides to add grab bars in the future — without requiring them to install the bars before they actually want or need them.

4. Rethink Kitchen Storage

Aging in place isn't just about mobility; it's also about making everyday tasks easier. Think about how often you reach into the back of a deep lower cabinet or climb onto a step stool to retrieve something from an upper shelf. Drawers, pull-out shelves, accessible pantry storage and thoughtfully placed appliances can reduce reaching, bending and searching while making a kitchen more enjoyable to use at any age.

This is one reason we encourage homeowners to think about how they actually use their kitchen during the design process — not simply where cabinets and appliances have traditionally been placed.

5. Don't Underestimate Good Lighting

Lighting is one of those remodeling decisions that can have an enormous impact without calling attention to itself.

Rather than relying on one overhead fixture, consider layers of lighting throughout the home: general room lighting, task lighting where you're preparing food or getting ready in the bathroom, under-cabinet lighting, and good illumination along hallways and stairs. Natural light can help, too.

A brighter home is generally easier to navigate and work in, and thoughtful lighting becomes even more important as our vision changes over time.

6. Think About What's Underfoot

Flooring decisions affect more than the way a room looks. During a remodel, consider traction, ease of maintenance and transitions between flooring materials. Wet areas such as bathrooms deserve particular attention, but abrupt changes in floor height or slippery surfaces can create challenges elsewhere in the home as well.

Ideally, flooring should create a smooth path from one area to another while still fitting the overall design of the home.

7. Choose Things That Are Easy to Operate

Sometimes the smallest choices make everyday life easier. Lever-style door handles can be easier to operate than round knobs. Cabinet drawers with easy-to-grasp pulls may be more comfortable than tiny knobs. Rocker-style light switches, user-friendly faucets and conveniently placed electrical outlets can all reduce unnecessary reaching or gripping.

None of these selections have to announce themselves as accessibility features. They're simply details that can make a home easier for a wide range of people to use.

That concept is closely related to universal design — creating spaces that work well for people of different ages and abilities rather than designing only for one particular stage of life.

8. Consider How the House Could Work Differently Someday

One of the biggest aging-in-place questions isn't about a particular fixture or finish. It's this:

Could this home still work for us if our needs changed?

For homeowners planning to remain in their home long-term, it can be worth considering whether essential living could eventually happen on one level. Is there a bedroom on the main floor? Is there a full bathroom nearby? Could an office, den or other flexible room serve a different purpose later? Is laundry reasonably accessible?

You don't necessarily need to remodel all of those spaces now. Sometimes simply considering future possibilities can help you avoid making decisions today that would make adapting the home much more difficult later.

You Don't Have to Do Everything at Once

Planning for aging in place doesn't mean trying to predict exactly what you'll need at 70, 80 or 90 years old. And it certainly doesn't mean your newly remodeled home needs to look like it was designed around limitations you don't currently have.

The goal is flexibility.

If you're opening walls, changing a floor plan, replacing cabinetry or completely rebuilding a bathroom anyway, it's worth asking one additional question during the design process:

Is there something we can do now that would make this space easier to use in the future?

Sometimes the answer costs very little during a remodel but would be considerably more difficult to change later.

Remodeling for the Way You Live — Now and Later

A thoughtful remodel should solve today's problems while considering how life might change in the years ahead.

At Renovations and Dependable Building, we help homeowners throughout Blacksburg, Christiansburg and the New River Valley think through the details that make a remodeled space both beautiful and functional — from layout and storage to lighting, fixtures and long-term usability.

If you're considering a kitchen, bathroom or whole-home remodeling project and want to create a home that works well for you now and in the years ahead, we'd be happy to start the conversation.

Updating a 1919 Sears Kit House for the Next Chapter

There’s something special about renovating an older home, particularly one with more than a century of history behind it.

For the owners of this 1919 Sears kit house in Pembroke, Virginia, the goal wasn’t to erase that history or make their home feel brand new. It was to make the spaces they use every day work better for the way they live now while thoughtfully preparing the home for the years ahead.

The result was actually two projects: a complete kitchen renovation and the addition of a large new back deck. Together, they’ve transformed how the homeowners can cook, entertain, relax, and enjoy their home in beautiful Giles County.

A Home Worth Staying In

Both homeowners work at local universities but they enjoy coming home to the quieter pace and beautiful surroundings of Giles County. They’re also a creative pair. She enjoys sewing, knitting, and other crafts, while he’s a musician. They love to cook, entertain friends, and host gatherings at home.

And, most importantly for the decisions behind this renovation, they’ve decided this is where they want to stay.

Rather than thinking only about what the house needs today, they’re gradually making improvements that will allow it to continue serving them comfortably as they get older. Some of those choices are subtle. Others — like adding a ramp to their new back deck — are much more visible.

That long-term perspective helped guide both projects.

Making a Small Kitchen Work Much Harder

The existing kitchen had served the house for many years, but it was ready for an update. Old wooden cabinetry provided limited organized storage, the overall style felt dated, and two people who genuinely enjoy cooking wanted better appliances, more usable counter space, and a kitchen that worked with them rather than against them.

Before: The original kitchen had dated wood cabinetry, limited organized storage, and less usable counter space for two homeowners who love to cook.

Because this is a historic home with smaller, defined rooms, the answer wasn’t to knock down walls and create an oversized kitchen with a massive island.

Instead, the goal was to make every inch of the existing kitchen work better.

The basic footprint remained recognizable, but we made some important changes. One window along the exterior wall was removed, allowing us to create significantly more uninterrupted counter space and cabinetry.

After: Creamy white cabinetry, additional counter space, improved storage, and a lighter color palette transformed the kitchen while preserving the home's original stained wood trim.

Creamy white cabinets now extend all the way to the ceiling. That gives the homeowners plenty of everyday storage while also creating space up high for items they use less frequently — a small design decision that makes a big difference in a compact kitchen. Inside the cabinetry, features including a traditional corner lazy Susan, pull-out pantry storage, and a double trash and recycling cabinet help keep everything organized and easy to access.

The result is a kitchen that feels brighter, more functional, and much more spacious without actually becoming a bigger room.

One of our favorite details: the home's original wide stained wood trim was carefully saved and reused, adding warmth and historic character to the updated kitchen.

Designing Around the Home’s Original Character

One of our favorite parts of this project is what didn’t change. The house still has its beautiful original stained wood trim: wide, substantial boards with the warmth and character that are difficult to reproduce in a newer home.

Rather than removing or painting it, we carefully saved and reused the original trim throughout the kitchen. That decision also influenced the new color palette.

The creamy cabinetry lightens the room without competing with the wood. The countertop and backsplash coordinate with one another, while the backsplash tile includes subtle touches of both blue and brown — tying together the blue walls and the rich tones of the original stained trim.

Instead of the historic wood feeling like something the new kitchen had to work around, it became part of the design.

That balance was important throughout the project: modernize the function without stripping away the personality of a 1919 home.

The backsplash was selected with the home's original woodwork in mind, with subtle blue and brown tones that connect the new finishes to the blue walls and rich stained trim.

A Few Surprises Come With a 107-Year-Old House

Anyone who has worked on an older home knows that opening the walls can reveal a few things that weren’t part of the original plan.

During demolition, we discovered an outdated and incorrectly configured plumbing connection serving the upstairs bathroom, which sits directly above the kitchen. It had to be corrected before we could continue moving forward. We also had to take extra care while removing the home’s old plaster and wood lath.

Renovating a 107-year-old home comes with a few surprises. Careful removal of the original plaster and wood lath was part of the process, and a salvaged exterior door helped us preserve the character of the house.

These aren’t the glamorous parts of a renovation (and they certainly aren’t the things you see in the finished photographs!) but addressing them properly is an important part of renovating an older home responsibly.

We also preserved other pieces of the home’s history wherever possible, including an original interior basement door. For an exterior door that needed to be replaced, we were able to find a salvaged door that better matched the character of the house.

Sometimes preserving an older home isn’t about restoring everything to exactly the way it looked in 1919. It’s about knowing which details are worth protecting and finding ways to let them coexist with the improvements a modern household needs.

The new two-level deck adds valuable outdoor living space, with a covered upper area for sheltered gatherings and an open lower level for enjoying the yard.

From a Concrete Pad to Outdoor Living Space

The kitchen wasn’t the only part of the home that needed to work harder.

Before this project, the back of the house opened onto a simple concrete pad. There wasn’t really a comfortable outdoor living area where the homeowners could sit, entertain, or enjoy the property. The new deck changed that completely.

We created two distinct levels: a covered upper deck that provides a protected outdoor living space and an open lower level that offers additional room to gather and enjoy the outdoors. A ramp was incorporated into the design as well.

Right now, it provides convenient access between the house and yard. Long term, it’s also one more way the homeowners are preparing the property to remain comfortable and accessible as they age.

That’s an approach to aging in place that we love: you don’t necessarily have to wait until you need a feature to add it. When accessibility can be incorporated naturally into a project you already want, it can simply become part of a beautiful, functional home.

The ramp was incorporated into the deck design to make access easier now while also supporting the homeowners’ long-term plan to age comfortably in the home.

More Room for the Life They Already Love

Although these projects added cabinetry, countertops, appliances, and a substantial amount of new outdoor square footage, the biggest change may be less tangible. 

The homeowners love cooking for friends and hosting gatherings. Now they have a kitchen that makes cooking together easier, offers significantly more usable storage and workspace, and feels bright and welcoming.

And just outside the kitchen, they have an entirely new place for people to gather. That connection between the indoor and outdoor spaces effectively expands the way the house can be used — without changing what makes this historic home feel like home.

For a couple who plans to stay here for many years, that was really the point. This renovation wasn’t about chasing trends or turning a 1919 Sears kit house into something it was never meant to be. It was about helping a well-loved home evolve.

More functional for today. More comfortable for tomorrow. And still unmistakably itself.

Planning a Remodel in the New River Valley?

If you love your home and your community but your space no longer works the way you need it to, you may not need a different house — you may just need to rethink the one you already have.

Knowing what to expect helps you plan a project that fits your budget and timeline. 
These guidelines are based on our most recent jobs in the area.
There are two ways to think about remodeling costs:
YOU CAN DESIGN TO A FIXED BUDGET:

If you have a firm budget in mind for your project, sharing that with us up front is critical so that we can suggest options that fit that budget. 

Note: Our focus is on delivering exceptional service and high-quality craftsmanship through our design-build approach. While we strive to provide value at every budget, our process and commitment to quality may not align with lower fixed budgets. We're dedicated to creating lasting results that reflect your vision and investment.

YOU CAN LET THE DESIGN DRIVE THE BUDGET:

If you have a flexible budget and are open to exploring possibilities, our design-and-budget consultation process is the perfect starting point.

This approach allows us to collaborate with you to develop a vision for your space, presenting creative solutions and tailored options to align with your goals.

Together, we’ll discover what’s possible while ensuring your investment reflects the quality and functionality you desire.

Small Bathroom

A compact space under 50 square feet, such as a powder room or guest bath, focusing on essential updates like fixtures, lighting, and maximizing storage. These usually include a small vanity and toilet.

Starting at $12,500
Mid-Size Bathroom

A space between 50-80 square feet, typically a standard full bathroom, offering room for upgrades like a new vanity, tilework, or enhanced lighting and ventilation.

Starting at $24,000
Large Bathroom

A spacious retreat over 100 square feet, such as a master ensuite, allowing for luxury features like a soaking tub, walk-in shower, custom cabinetry, and high-end finishes. May include a separate toilet room and closet.

Starting at $46,000
Planning a Remodel?
Take the Guide With You

Our free Bathroom & Kitchen Remodeling Cost Guide goes beyond the numbers, with budgeting tips, project-planning guidance, and what to expect as you prepare for a renovation.

Get the Free Guide
Small Kitchen

A compact space typically 70-100 square feet, 30 square feet of countertop, 10-12 cabinets. Ideal for condos or smaller homes, focused on maximizing functionality with efficient layouts and minimal cabinetry.

Starting at $55,000
Mid-Size Kitchen

A versatile space between 100-200 sq ft, 55 sq ft of countertop, 15-18 cabinets, and a mid-sized island, offering room for upgraded appliances, additional cabinetry, and a mix of style and functionality.

Starting at $85,000
Large Kitchen

A spacious layout with 200+ sq ft, 75 sq ft of countertop, and 18-25 cabinets. Perfect for entertaining, with room for luxury features like a large island, high-end appliances, custom design elements, and upscale finishes.

Starting at $125,000
Other Projects
Office, Den, Basement, and Attic

Beyond kitchens and bathrooms, we specialize in transforming a variety of spaces to fit your lifestyle and needs. Whether it’s creating a functional home office, designing a cozy den, finishing a basement for added living space, or updating a bedroom for a more modern feel, we bring the same commitment to quality craftsmanship and thoughtful design. No matter the project, our goal is to create spaces that are both beautiful and practical, enhancing the comfort and value of your home.

​

Note that kitchens and bathrooms are the most expensive rooms to remodel. Other rooms, like bedrooms and living rooms, require less materials (no pricey cabinets and fixtures!), less labor, and are faster to complete.
